rationale: This is the control in batch 2 that turns out not to be a refusal, and it separates from the eighteen for a reason that generalises: its subject is a DOCUMENT, not an act performed on a person. Upstream says so in its own rationale — a contingency plan is developed, distributed, coordinated, reviewed and updated — and the first of those verbs produces an artifact of exactly the class the wave-1 `documents` collector was built for, on the same argument that made AC-01 and SA-05 partial rather than narrative. A repository is a document store under version control with a content hash per commit, so a declared contingency plan can be shown to exist at the path the repository named, to be non-empty, and to be anchored to the commit so that a later edit kills the evidence rather than passing unnoticed. Anchoring is a property of the EVIDENCE and not a limb of the control, which is the discipline AC-01 and SA-05 kept and the line this record nearly crossed: a hash detects a modification after the fact rather than restricting who may make one, and no assertion can even read it, since the collector emits present, bytes and non_empty while the content hash rides the bundle as an anchor rather than as an observation field. The route also may not ride the existing `system-documentation` kind, whose subject is SA-05's administrator, user and operations documentation — a `contingency-plan` kind is a schema change, a new recipe and this adjudication link, which is the process the documents schema states in its own comment and the same obligation the PL-08 record carries. What is reached is the existence and integrity of a document the system is asked to develop; the remainder names everything else. The disposition is partial and stays partial — N0 decision 3 — so this control remains uncovered and adds one to the authoring backlog rather than to the coverage figure.

remainder.control: Everything the control asks for beyond the file being there. The collector reads a path, a size and a content hash and does not read the document, so whether the plan identifies essential mission and business functions, states recovery objectives and restoration priorities, or addresses maintaining function through a disruption is the adequacy limb this plane never claims. Distribution to key personnel and coordination with incident handling are acts performed on people and leave no trace in a checkout. And the review cycle — reviewed on a defined frequency, updated after changes, changes communicated — is the currency limb this overlay has repeatedly had to name as an absence: no collector emits git-history metadata any assertion can read — gitleaks walks the full committed history and reports the rule, the file, the line and the commit a leak sits at, and nothing else dates a path, enumerates its edits or resolves who reviewed one, so a plan committed once and abandoned reads identically to one reviewed last week. Three further limbs are named rather than left to the catch-all, because each is a place a reader could assume the route reaches further than it does. CP-02 (h) asks that the plan be protected from unauthorized DISCLOSURE and modification, and the route reaches neither half: a content hash is detective rather than restrictive on the modification half, and on the disclosure half committing the plan into the repository is neutral at best and adverse at worst, since it widens the set of readers rather than narrowing it. CP-02 (a)(7) asks that the plan be reviewed and approved by designated officials, which is an approval event outside the checkout. And CP-02 (g) asks that lessons learned from testing and from actual events be incorporated, which is the CP-04 subject this overlay refuses outright.
remainder.boundary: rampscan enumerates from the checkout it was handed and multi-repo joins are deferred by name, so nothing here knows the scanned repository is the whole authorization boundary. The plan may be maintained in a second repository, in a document management system, or in the binder a 3PAO reads, and an evidenced row means the declared file was found where the declaration pointed — never that the declaration is the complete set.

citesUpstream.note: Upstream refuses and this record does not, and the divergence is the clean case rather than an argument about the same evidence. Their sentence is that a 3PAO reads the plan, its distribution list and its revision history, and that no API reports a plan exists or that anyone maintains it. Every clause of that is correct about an estate API and the first clause stops being correct the moment the reader is a source collector: a plan committed to the repository IS readable, and its existence, its non-emptiness and its integrity against a named commit are exactly what this plane signs. So the divergence is narrow and should be read narrowly — it is one limb of one verb, `develop`, plus the protection-from-modification limb their rationale does not reach. On distribution and on maintenance this record does not diverge at all; it concedes both in its remainder in the same terms they use. What a reader holding both overlays should take is not that one pass was wrong, but that the artifact upstream correctly says no API reports is a file, and there is now a plane that reads files.

externalSystem: Nothing. Collectors take no network by decision, execution is local, and signing is node:crypto. The distinction matters on a contingency control because the alternative evidence path is a document management or GRC platform holding the plan and its distribution list, and adopting one puts a system of record for recovery procedures inside the boundary being recovered. Reading the plan out of the checkout adds nothing: the file is already in the repository the assessment is about.
